claims.text: A dual-phase nanostructure governs the strong magnetocaloric response in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
The relevant dual-phase nanostructure consists of nanometer-scale intermetallic precipitates embedded in a homogeneous matrix.
Nanometer-scale intermetallic precipitates create localized regions with modified magnetic exchange interactions.
The precipitate-containing nanostructure enhances phonon-mediated thermal transport.
A controlled minor alloying addition or heat treatment can induce dispersed nanoscale intermetallic precipitates without significantly changing overall composition.
Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates and associated grain-boundary regions mediate magnetic exchange fluctuations.
Nanoscale intermetallic precipitates and associated grain-boundary regions mediate phonon heat conduction.
Local modification of magnetic exchange interactions by the precipitates increases magnetic entropy change at low applied fields.
The precipitates provide efficient pathways for phonon-mediated heat transport.
The combined magnetic and thermal roles of the precipitates produce a pronounced magnetocaloric effect with minimal thermal hysteresis.
The combined magnetic and thermal roles of the precipitates preserve mechanical stability.
Relative to a homogeneous single-phase baseline, controlled precipitate formation will increase magnetic entropy change at low applied fields.
Relative to the baseline, controlled precipitate formation will reduce thermal hysteresis.
Relative to the baseline, controlled precipitate formation will maintain or improve mechanical properties.
The proposed mechanism should hold at precipitate volume fractions of approximately 2–10%.
The proposed mechanism should hold over temperature and magnetic-field ranges typical of magnetic refrigeration.
No direct eligible evidence supports the proposed mechanism in rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys.
The applicability of the mechanism to rare-earth-free high-entropy alloys remains to be experimentally validated.
